data.why: A nuclear bunker built the way the account builds things: a deep hole in a yard section, where rain floods it and the walls cave in, then concrete walls, a roof slab, soil and a steel blast door fix it one problem at a time. Each fix opens the next problem: the sealed room goes stale, so an air pipe goes in, and then a blast wave can rush down that pipe, so a valve slams it shut. The camera opens close on the hole, widens to the whole cut, uses number counters beside the soil for the radiation facts, and ends on the calm finished bunker with a ceiling light, bunk beds and grass on top.

ideas.idea: you start with the naive thing: dig a deep hole in your yard and call it a bunker
the first storm runs off the lawn and pours straight into the open hole
the hole fills to the brim like a bathtub
wet soil is heavy, over 100 pounds a cubic foot, so the walls crack and cave in
you pump it dry and pour a concrete floor and walls to hold the soil back
you cap the box with a thick roof slab and pile three feet of soil on top
you hang a steel blast door on the only way in; the biggest ones weigh 25 tons
this sealed box of concrete, soil and steel is a nuclear bunker
soil and concrete soak up the radiation while the door and roof stop the blast wave
three feet of packed soil cuts gamma rays by a factor of about 1000
sealed in, the people breathe and the air goes stale
a filter and a fan pull fresh air down a pipe from outside
that pipe is a hole in the shield, and a blast wave would rush straight down it
a blast valve on the pipe slams shut when the shock arrives
everyone pictures hiding underground for years, but that is not what a bunker is for
fallout fades fast: after about 49 hours the radiation is down to around one percent
add a ceiling light, bunk beds and the grass back on top to finish the shelter
a calm, finished bunker under a quiet lawn
